clinicalPearls: Deficient secretion of growth hormone with otherwise intact pituitary hormones, presenting as proportionate postnatal growth failure with a slow growth velocity
Genetic forms involve GH1 (growth hormone gene) or GHRHR (growth-hormone-releasing-hormone receptor) mutations, and inheritance may be recessive, dominant, or X-linked depending on subtype
Both growth hormone and IGF-1 are low, distinguishing it from Laron syndrome where growth hormone is high and IGF-1 is low
Affected children may show truncal adiposity, a youthful or immature face, and delayed bone age, and infants can present with hypoglycaemia
Diagnosis relies on growth-hormone stimulation testing alongside low IGF-1 and IGF binding protein-3
Growth hormone replacement is effective and, when started early, can substantially improve growth and often final height
Some type IA cases develop antibodies to growth hormone during replacement, blunting the response
Pituitary imaging and screening for additional deficiencies help distinguish isolated from combined pituitary hormone deficiency
reference.pathophysiology: Isolated growth hormone deficiency arises when the somatotroph axis fails to produce adequate growth hormone while other anterior pituitary functions remain intact. Genetic causes include mutations in the growth hormone gene (GH1) or the growth-hormone-releasing-hormone receptor (GHRHR), and acquired cases follow structural, inflammatory, or idiopathic hypothalamic-pituitary disease. Because growth hormone drives hepatic IGF-1 production and skeletal growth, its deficiency lowers IGF-1 and slows linear growth, and in infancy the loss of growth hormone's counter-regulatory action can cause hypoglycaemia. Unlike growth hormone insensitivity, the receptor and downstream signalling are intact, so exogenous growth hormone restores IGF-1 and promotes growth.
additionalDifferentials: Laron syndrome and growth hormone insensitivity
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
Turner syndrome and other chromosomal causes
additionalInvestigations: IGF-1 and IGF binding protein-3 (both low)
Assessment of other pituitary axes to exclude combined deficiency
MRI of the hypothalamic-pituitary region for structural lesions
Genetic testing of GH1 and GHRHR in familial or early cases
redFlags: Neonatal hypoglycaemia, prolonged jaundice, or micropenis suggesting hypopituitarism
Rapidly declining growth velocity crossing centiles
Features of an intracranial mass such as headache or visual disturbance
Evidence of additional pituitary hormone deficiencies
reference.prognosis: With timely growth hormone replacement the growth outlook is good and many children reach a height within the normal range; prognosis worsens when treatment is delayed or when the deficiency is part of broader pituitary disease.
pitfalls: Confusing it with growth hormone insensitivity by not measuring IGF-1 and growth hormone together
Overlooking additional pituitary deficiencies that need replacement
Missing an underlying structural lesion by omitting pituitary imaging
Attributing short stature to constitutional delay without adequate testing
Not recognising anti-growth-hormone antibodies as a cause of poor response in certain genetic subtypes
references: Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance on growth hormone deficiency
management: Recombinant human growth hormone replacement, started early to maximise linear growth and final adult height
Management of neonatal and infantile hypoglycaemia arising from loss of growth hormone counter-regulation
Monitoring of growth velocity, IGF-1 and IGF binding protein-3 to titrate dosing and confirm treatment response
Surveillance for treatment side effects alongside periodic bone-age assessment
Reassessment of the somatotroph axis at completion of linear growth to determine the need for adult growth hormone replacement
Genetic counselling in familial or early-onset cases associated with GH1 or GHRHR variants
Endocrinology referral for stimulation testing, diagnostic confirmation and long-term supervision
